## In 60 seconds

An electrogram is the voltage an electrode picks up from currents crossing cell membranes
nearby. A **unipolar** electrogram measures one electrode against a distant reference. It sees
the local wavefront clearly, but it also sees activity far away. A **bipolar** electrogram
subtracts two nearby unipolar signals. That subtraction acts like a spatial derivative: it keeps
sharp local detail and cancels slowly varying, distant activity. The price is direction
dependence. A bipole aligned with the wave records a large signal; a bipole turned across it
records almost nothing. An **omnipolar** signal combines several bipoles to estimate the local
electric field, then reads it along the direction the wave is travelling, which removes most of
that dependence. Height above the tissue, electrode size and electrode spacing all act as
spatial filters on what the catheter can see.

## From the field

Practical lessons reported from mapping labs, each tied to the part of this module that
explains it.

- **Use unipolar and bipolar recordings together.** A review of recording techniques describes
  minimally filtered unipolar recordings as useful for mapping a **focal source** (a small region
  from which activation spreads outward), but notes that their far-field signal can hide small
  local signals in diseased tissue. Bipolar recordings are standard because they reject far-field
  signal. Still, the local signal can come from under either electrode, far-field signals do
  appear, and unipolar recordings taken at the same time help in some situations [@stevenson2005]. The physics is in
  @eq-m03-farfield.
- **Filtering changes what a unipolar signal can tell you.** High-pass filtering a unipolar
  recording reduces its far-field part but limits what its shape can tell you [@stevenson2005].
  Module m04 covers the recording chain and its filters.
- **Catheter orientation changes bipolar voltage.** In sheep with a **myocardial infarction** (heart
  muscle killed by loss of its blood supply), a grid catheter compared two bipoles at each site
  that shared the same center and spacing but crossed at right angles. Their voltages differed by a
  median of 31.7%, and by 48.7% where the wavefront ran perpendicular to one bipole and parallel to
  the other. Sites between 0.5 and 1.5 mV were the most likely to change voltage range: only 55.8%
  stayed in the same range [@takigawa2018]. Demo m03-d2 and @eq-m03-bipolar-gradient show why.
- **Smaller, closer electrodes see more inside low-voltage areas.** A **low-voltage area** is a
  region whose bipolar voltage falls below a chosen cut-off; it is often read as **scar** (fibrous
  tissue that has replaced heart muscle). In patients with scar-related **arrhythmias** (abnormal heart rhythms) of the **atria** (the
  upper chambers of the heart), a
  catheter with 1-mm electrodes measured a smaller area below 0.5 mV than one with a 3.5-mm tip
  (14.7 versus 20.4 cm²) and higher voltages inside it (0.28 versus 0.17 mV). It also found distinct,
  timeable electrograms at 54.4% of low-voltage points, against 21.4% for the larger tip
  [@anter2015]. The catheters differed in both electrode size and spacing, so this is their
  combined effect; @eq-m03-disk-average and demo m03-d3 show both filters.
- **Omnipoles reduce orientation effects in real maps.** In isolated rabbit, pig and human hearts,
  bipolar voltage maps made along two perpendicular electrode orientations differed by an average
  of 0.25 ± 0.18 mV in the human hearts. Omnipolar voltages were steadier from beat to beat
  (coefficient of variation 0.08 versus 0.28 for bipoles, in human hearts) [@magtibay2017]. See
  @eq-m03-omnipole and demo m03-d5.


## Derivations

**Symbols used throughout.** $\sigma$ extracellular conductivity (S/m). $i_m$ membrane current
per unit area of tissue, positive outward (A/m²). $V_m$ transmembrane voltage. $h$ electrode
height above the tissue (mm). $w$ width of the activation front (mm). $c$ conduction velocity
(m/s, which equals mm/ms). $\hat n$ unit vector along the direction of propagation. $d$
interelectrode spacing (mm). $\hat u$ unit vector along a bipole, from its proximal to its distal
electrode. $\theta$ angle between $\hat u$ and $\hat n$. $k$ spatial frequency (rad/mm).

### Where a unipolar electrogram comes from

The extracellular electrogram is produced by transmembrane currents that flow out into the
extracellular space as the impulse propagates [@debakker2019]. A unipolar recording measures the
potential at one exploring electrode relative to a distant reference electrode.

To compute that potential, treat the tissue and blood as an infinite, homogeneous, isotropic
conductor, and treat the fields as quasi-static. A membrane current density then produces a
potential that falls off as one over distance [@plonsey2007]. For a thin sheet of tissue in the
plane $z = 0$:

$$
\phi(\mathbf r, t) = \frac{1}{4\pi\sigma} \iint \frac{i_m(\mathbf r', t)}{\lVert \mathbf r - \mathbf r' \rVert}\, dA'
$$ {#eq-m03-volume-conductor}

**Membrane current from the voltage profile.** Along a thin strand, the intracellular current is
$I_i = -\beta\,\partial V_m/\partial x$, where $\beta$ (S) lumps the intracellular conductivity and the
sheet thickness. If the extracellular potential gradient is small next to the intracellular one,
current conservation says the outward membrane current equals the loss of intracellular current
along the strand, $i_m = -\partial I_i/\partial x$, so

$$
i_m = \beta\,\frac{\partial^2 V_m}{\partial x^2}
$$ {#eq-m03-cable}

**A wavefront with a closed form.** Let a planar front travel along $+x$ at speed $c$. Write
$s = x - ct$ for the signed distance from the front: $s > 0$ is tissue the front has not reached
yet. Model the rise of $V_m$ across the front with an arctangent profile of width $w$ and
amplitude $\Delta V$:

$$
V_m(s) = \Delta V \left( \tfrac12 - \tfrac1\pi \arctan\frac{s}{w} \right),
\qquad
\frac{dV_m}{ds} = -\frac{\Delta V}{\pi}\,\frac{w}{s^2 + w^2}
$$ {#eq-m03-front}

The slope is a Lorentzian of width $w$. Its second derivative is odd in $s$: outward current
(a source) ahead of the front, inward current (a sink) behind it. Net membrane current over the
whole front is zero.

**The height filter.** Take the Fourier transform of @eq-m03-volume-conductor in the plane of the
sheet. The kernel $1/\sqrt{\rho^2 + h^2}$ transforms to $2\pi e^{-|k| h}/|k|$, so

$$
\hat\phi(k) = \frac{e^{-|k| h}}{2\sigma |k|}\, \hat i_m(k)
$$ {#eq-m03-height-filter}

The factor $e^{-|k|h}$ is a spatial low-pass filter. The farther the electrode sits from the
tissue, the more fine spatial detail it loses.

**The unipolar electrogram.** Insert @eq-m03-cable and @eq-m03-front into
@eq-m03-height-filter. For a planar front only the spatial frequency along $x$ matters, so $k$ is
one-dimensional. Since $\hat i_m = -\beta k^2 \hat V_m$ and the transform of
$dV_m/ds$ is $-\Delta V e^{-w|k|}$, the potential spectrum is
$\hat\phi = -i\,\mathrm{sgn}(k)\,\frac{\beta\Delta V}{2\sigma}\, e^{-(w+h)|k|}$. Its inverse
transform is

$$
U(s) = A\,\frac{s}{s^2 + a^2},
\qquad
A = \frac{\beta\,\Delta V}{2\pi\sigma},
\qquad
a = w + h
$$ {#eq-m03-unipolar-closed}

Read it as a waveform in time at a fixed electrode, where $s = x_e - ct$:

- Before the front arrives ($s > 0$) the potential is positive. It peaks at $s = a$.
- It falls through zero exactly as the front passes under the electrode ($s = 0$).
- After the front passes ($s < 0$) it is negative, with its trough at $s = -a$.
- Peak-to-peak amplitude is $A/a = A/(w + h)$. Moving the electrode away from the tissue, or
  widening the front, shrinks the signal.

**Slope and the intrinsic deflection.** By the chain rule,

$$
\frac{dU}{dt} = -c\,\frac{dU}{ds}
$$ {#eq-m03-unipolar-slope}

so the unipolar slope scales with conduction velocity. In this model the steepest negative slope
is $-cA/a^2$, and it occurs exactly at $s = 0$, when the front passes the electrode. That is the
basis of the classic marker of **local activation time**, the moment the front reaches the
electrode:

$$
t_{\text{act}} \approx \arg\max_t \left( -\frac{dU}{dt} \right)
$$ {#eq-m03-intrinsic-deflection}

Simulation work predicts that this "intrinsic deflection" matches the steepest rise of the action
potential, with small errors under ideal uniform propagation. It errs more near changes in
activation sequence, short strands and non-uniform coupling [@steinhaus1989]. Our model is the
ideal case, so the match is exact.

::: {.demo #m03-d1 badge="approximate model"}
```{=html}
<div id="m03-d1-root" class="demo-root" data-demo="m03-d1"></div>
<script type="module" src="../demos/m03-d1-unipolar.js"></script>
```

**Assumptions**

- Model: the arctangent front of @eq-m03-front in a thin tissue sheet, seen by a point electrode in an infinite homogeneous conductor (@eq-m03-unipolar-closed). It ignores the blood–tissue boundary, anisotropy, curved fronts and amplifier filtering.
- Default conduction velocity 1.0 m/s, reported for the anterior left atrial wall in normal-voltage areas; low-voltage areas in the same study averaged 0.6 m/s [@heil2023].
- Default electrode height 1 mm, the electrode-to-tissue distance used in a published omnipolar simulation [@riccio2021].
- Default front width 0.3 mm. From @eq-m03-front, the fastest upstroke is $c\,\Delta V/(\pi w)$, so $w = c\,\Delta V/(\pi \max dV_m/dt)$. Human right atrial trabeculae had an action-potential amplitude $\Delta V$ of about 95–99 mV [@loose2014]. With an upstroke of about 100 V/s in human atrial fibres [@wang1991] and $c$ = 1 m/s, $w \approx$ 0.3 mm. The trabeculae study itself reported 250–300 V/s, which gives $w \approx$ 0.1 mm. Because $h$ = 1 mm dominates $a = w + h$, that range changes $a$ by only 0.2 mm; set the front-width slider to 0.1 mm to compare (arithmetic checked in `tests/test_m03_unipolar.py`).
- Amplitudes are relative. The scale $A$ depends on tissue properties not modeled here, so the readout compares with the defaults.
- What would change the result: non-ideal propagation moves the steepest downstroke away from true activation [@steinhaus1989].
:::

**Key takeaways**

- A unipolar electrogram is a weighted sum of membrane currents, weighted by one over distance.
- For a passing planar front it is positive, then crosses zero at activation, then is negative.
- Its amplitude falls as $1/(w + h)$; its steepest slope scales with $c/(w + h)^2$.
- The steepest downstroke marks activation exactly only in ideal propagation.

### The bipolar electrogram as a spatial difference

A bipolar electrogram is the difference between two unipolar signals. We use the convention
distal minus proximal:

$$
V_{\text{bip}}(t) = \phi(\mathbf r_1, t) - \phi(\mathbf r_2, t),
\qquad
\mathbf r_{1,2} = \mathbf r_0 \pm \tfrac{d}{2}\,\hat u
$$ {#eq-m03-bipolar}

For a planar wave, only the distance of each electrode along $\hat n$ matters. The two electrodes
sit at $s \pm \delta$ with $\delta = \tfrac{d}{2}\cos\theta$, so

$$
V_{\text{bip}}(s) = U(s + \delta) - U(s - \delta)
$$ {#eq-m03-bipolar-planar}

**A close bipole is a directional derivative.** When $d$ is small next to $a$, expand to first
order:

$$
V_{\text{bip}} \approx d\, \hat u \cdot \nabla \phi = d \cos\theta\, \frac{dU}{ds}
$$ {#eq-m03-bipolar-gradient}

The relative error of this approximation falls as $d^2$. Three consequences follow:

- **Direction dependence.** Amplitude scales with $|\cos\theta|$. A bipole perpendicular to the
  direction of propagation ($\theta = 90°$) records nothing, because both electrodes activate
  together. In animal recordings, voltage at the same site varied most where the wavefront was
  perpendicular to one bipole and parallel to the other [@takigawa2018].
- **Amplitude.** Using $dU/ds$ from @eq-m03-unipolar-closed, the peak-to-peak bipolar amplitude
  tends to $d\,|\cos\theta| \cdot 9A/(8a^2)$ as $d \to 0$.
- **Locality.** Unipolar amplitude falls as $1/a$, but bipolar amplitude falls as $1/a^2$. The
  bipole is dominated by tissue closer to the catheter.

::: {.demo #m03-d2 badge="approximate model"}
```{=html}
<div id="m03-d2-root" class="demo-root" data-demo="m03-d2"></div>
<script type="module" src="../demos/m03-d2-bipole-orientation.js"></script>
```

**Assumptions**

- Model: two point electrodes at $\pm d/2$ along the bipole axis and the planar arctangent front (@eq-m03-bipolar-planar). It ignores electrode size (see m03-d3), curved fronts and the blood–tissue boundary.
- Default spacing 2 mm, the bipole spacing of a 2-5-2 mm **decapolar** (ten-electrode) catheter [@iafdb]. Height 1 mm [@riccio2021] and conduction velocity 1.0 m/s [@heil2023] as in m03-d1; front width as in m03-d1.
- The polar plot divides by an aligned bipole of the same spacing, so it shows direction dependence only.
- What would change the result: curved or colliding wavefronts, and slow conduction zones under one electrode.
:::

**Key takeaways**

- A bipole measures a spatial difference; when it is short, that is a directional derivative.
- Bipolar amplitude depends on catheter orientation and on spacing, not only on the tissue.
- A bipole is more local than a unipole: its amplitude falls off faster with distance.

### Recordings as spatial filters

@eq-m03-height-filter already showed that distance from the tissue is a low-pass filter. Two more
filters complete the picture.

**Electrode size.** A disk electrode of radius $r_e$ reports, approximately, the average potential
over its face. Averaging a spatial harmonic over a disk multiplies it by

$$
H_{\text{disk}}(k) = \frac{2 J_1(k r_e)}{k r_e}
$$ {#eq-m03-disk-average}

where $J_1$ is the Bessel function of the first kind. This is another low-pass filter: larger
electrodes blur fine detail. The model ignores contact effects and current shunting by the metal.

**The bipole.** Apply @eq-m03-bipolar to a harmonic $e^{i k\, \hat n \cdot \mathbf r}$:

$$
H_{\text{bip}}(k) = 2i \sin\!\left( \frac{k d \cos\theta}{2} \right),
\qquad
|H_{\text{bip}}| = 2 \left| \sin\!\left( \frac{k d \cos\theta}{2} \right) \right|
$$ {#eq-m03-bipolar-transfer}

This is a spatial high-pass filter. It rejects slowly varying fields ($k \to 0$), peaks near
$k d \cos\theta = \pi$, and has nulls wherever $k d \cos\theta$ is a multiple of $2\pi$.

Put together, a bipolar recording sees the tissue's current pattern through
$H_{\text{bip}} \cdot H_{\text{disk}} \cdot e^{-|k|h}$: a spatial band-pass filter. Height and
electrode size set the upper edge; spacing sets the lower edge and the nulls.

**Far-field rejection.** A distant source changes slowly across the catheter, so the bipole
mostly cancels it. For a distant point source the unipole falls off as $1/R$ and a bipole as
$1/R^2$; for a distant dipole, as $1/R^2$ and $1/R^3$:

$$
\phi_{\text{monopole}} \propto \frac{1}{R},\quad V_{\text{bip}} \propto \frac{d}{R^2};
\qquad
\phi_{\text{dipole}} \propto \frac{1}{R^2},\quad V_{\text{bip}} \propto \frac{d}{R^3}
$$ {#eq-m03-farfield}

This is why bipolar recordings reject far-field signal better than unipolar ones. They do not
remove it completely: far-field signals still appear in bipolar recordings, and the local signal
can lie under either electrode [@stevenson2005].

::: {.demo #m03-d3 badge="exact"}
```{=html}
<div id="m03-d3-root" class="demo-root" data-demo="m03-d3"></div>
<script type="module" src="../demos/m03-d3-transfer-functions.js"></script>
```

**Assumptions**

- Each curve is a closed-form result: @eq-m03-height-filter, @eq-m03-disk-average and @eq-m03-bipolar-transfer for a bipole aligned with the wave ($\theta$ = 0), plotted as $|H|/2$ so its maximum is 1.
- The disk model assumes the electrode reports the average potential over a flat disk. It ignores current shunting by the metal and partial contact.
- Default spacing 2 mm [@iafdb] and height 1 mm [@riccio2021]. Default radius 0.5 mm treats a 1-mm electrode [@anter2015] as a 1-mm-diameter disk; real electrodes are often rings or tips.
:::

::: {.demo #m03-d4 badge="approximate model"}
```{=html}
<div id="m03-d4-root" class="demo-root" data-demo="m03-d4"></div>
<script type="module" src="../demos/m03-d4-far-field.js"></script>
```

**Assumptions**

- Local signal: as in m03-d2, with the bipole aligned with the wave and 2-mm spacing [@iafdb].
- Far source: one current dipole on the bipole axis, pointing along it, with a biphasic time course 25 ms after local activation. Its strength is set so that at 20 mm it equals the local unipolar signal. These are illustrative choices, not physiological values; only the trend with distance is meant (@eq-m03-farfield).
- Each panel is scaled by its own local peak-to-peak, so the panels compare the far-field share, not absolute size.
- What would change the result: a far source off the bipole axis or a bipole across it (less bipolar pickup), and conductivity boundaries such as the blood–tissue interface.
:::

**Key takeaways**

- Distance and electrode size are spatial low-pass filters; a bipole is a spatial high-pass filter.
- A bipolar recording is therefore a spatial band-pass filter, tuned by height, size and spacing.
- Bipoles reject distant sources better than unipoles, but not completely.

### Omnipolar signals from a clique of electrodes

An omnipolar method estimates the local electric field from a small group of electrodes, called a
**clique**, and reads it along the direction of propagation [@deno2017; @riccio2021].

**The field from a clique.** The electric field is $\mathbf E = -\nabla\phi$. If the potential is
nearly linear across the clique, each bipole between electrodes $i$ and $j$ is a projection of
the field, $b_{ij} = \phi_j - \phi_i \approx -(\mathbf r_j - \mathbf r_i) \cdot \mathbf E$.
Stack the bipoles into a vector $\mathbf b$ and the electrode separations into the columns of a
matrix $D$. Then $\mathbf b = -D^{\mathsf T}\mathbf E$, and the least-squares estimate
is [@riccio2021]

$$
\hat{\mathbf E}(t) = -\left( D D^{\mathsf T} \right)^{-1} D\, \mathbf b(t)
$$ {#eq-m03-clique-field}

A triangle of three electrodes or a square of four can be used. For a linear potential the
estimate is exact.

**The omnipolar signal.** For a plane wave the field points along $\pm\hat n$ at every instant, so
$\hat{\mathbf E}(t)$ traces a line, not a loop, along the propagation direction [@riccio2021].
Reading the field along a unit direction $\hat\omega$ gives the signal a bipole of spacing $d$
would record if it pointed that way:

$$
v_\omega(t) = -d\, \hat\omega \cdot \hat{\mathbf E}(t)
$$ {#eq-m03-omnipole}

With $\hat\omega = \hat n$, this equals an aligned bipole, whatever the catheter's orientation.
Here we take $\hat\omega$ as the principal axis of the field loop. The published method instead
picks the angle whose field projection best matches the time derivative of the unipolar signal
[@riccio2021], following @deno2017. For a plane wave both choices give $\hat n$.

**Velocity from one clique.** Along $\hat n$ the field is $-dU/ds$, while the unipolar slope is
$-c\, dU/ds$ (@eq-m03-unipolar-slope). Their ratio gives the conduction velocity without
measuring activation times [@riccio2021; @deno2017]:

$$
c \approx \frac{\mathrm{pp}\left( dU/dt \right)}{\mathrm{pp}\left( \hat n \cdot \hat{\mathbf E} \right)}
$$ {#eq-m03-clique-velocity}

where pp is the peak-to-peak amplitude. Module m25 returns to this.

**Where it breaks down.** The estimate assumes the wave is planar and the potential is linear
inside the clique. Neither holds when the spacing is not small next to $a = w + h$. In our model,
without time alignment, the spread of omnipolar amplitude across 18 wave directions grows from
under 1% at $d/a = 0.2$ to about 32% at $d/a = 1.6$ for a square clique, and more for a triangle
(computed with `labs/python/epml`; the trend is checked in `tests/test_m03_omnipolar.py`). Published work reports the same mechanism:
bipoles within a clique activate at slightly different times, which biases the estimate, and
aligning them first reduces the bias [@riccio2021]. Curved or colliding wavefronts make the field
trace a true loop, and no single direction then describes propagation.

::: {.demo #m03-d5 badge="approximate model"}
```{=html}
<div id="m03-d5-root" class="demo-root" data-demo="m03-d5"></div>
<script type="module" src="../demos/m03-d5-omnipole.js"></script>
```

**Assumptions**

- Model: the planar arctangent front crossing a square clique of point electrodes. The field comes from all six bipoles by least squares (@eq-m03-clique-field), and the omnipole reads it along the loop's principal axis (@eq-m03-omnipole).
- The published method picks the direction by cross-correlation with the unipolar derivative and can time-align the bipoles first [@riccio2021]. Neither is done here, which is why the omnipole is not perfectly direction-independent at larger spacing.
- Default spacing 2 mm, the grid spacing in a published omnipolar simulation, and height 1 mm from the same study [@riccio2021]; front width as in m03-d1. With these defaults $d/a$ is about 1.5. Reduce the spacing to see the omnipole become direction-independent.
- What would change the result: time alignment, curved wavefronts (the loop opens up) and noise.
:::

**Key takeaways**

- A clique of electrodes estimates the local electric field by least squares.
- Reading that field along the propagation direction removes most orientation dependence.
- The method assumes a locally planar wave; it degrades as spacing grows relative to $w + h$.

## Clinical correlate

::: {.callout-note title="Pending clinical review"}
This section describes published findings only. It is not guidance for patient care, and it has
not yet been reviewed by an EP physician.
:::

**Why the same tissue can look normal or low voltage.** Bipolar voltage maps are used to outline
scar, for example in studies of **ventricular tachycardia** (a fast rhythm that starts in the
lower chambers of the heart) [@marchlinski2000]. In that study, normal **endocardium** (the inner
surface of the heart wall) was defined as a bipolar amplitude above 1.5 mV, based on maps in
**sinus rhythm** (the normal heartbeat) from 6 patients without structural heart disease, and
"dense scar" as below 0.5 mV [@marchlinski2000]. Those values were set with the catheters and
mapping system of that study. The same two values appear in later studies
[@takigawa2018; @magtibay2017].

This module shows why a cut-off cannot be separated from the instrument. A close bipole's
amplitude is $\frac{9A}{8a^2}\, d\, \lvert\cos\theta\rvert$: it depends on the source strength
$A$, but also on $w + h$, the spacing $d$ and the angle $\theta$ to the wavefront, and the
electrode size filters it further (see the cheat sheet). Published studies show each effect:

- **Orientation.** At the same sites, two crossing bipoles of equal spacing put many points in
  different voltage ranges, most often between 0.5 and 1.5 mV [@takigawa2018].
- **Electrode size and spacing.** Two catheters gave similar normal atrial values (fifth
  percentiles 0.48 and 0.52 mV), yet in scarred atria the smaller, closer electrodes measured a
  smaller low-voltage area [@anter2015].
- **Recording method.** A study of omnipolar voltage set its own threshold from **ablation** lesions (small areas of tissue destroyed on purpose, here by
  radiofrequency heating) in pig hearts. Maps using the traditional bipolar dense-scar cut-off of 0.5 mV outlined those
  lesions poorly [@magtibay2017].

An editorial asks the question directly: what does bipolar voltage amplitude really mean
[@anter2016]? The engineering answer from this module: it describes the tissue *as seen by a
particular catheter, at a particular orientation, for a particular wavefront*. Module m23 covers
voltage mapping.

**Assumptions**

- Schematic: the curves use the module's formulas with illustrative parameter values
  (@eq-m03-height-filter, @eq-m03-disk-average, @eq-m03-bipolar-transfer). They are not to scale
  and make no quantitative claim. The tissue sketch shows the shape of $\partial^2 V_m/\partial x^2$ for the

- The chain is the module's model: a thin tissue sheet, an infinite homogeneous conductor and a
  planar front. Demo m03-d3 plots the same factors with real units.

## How experts think

Treat every electrogram as a measurement of the tissue *through an instrument*. Before reading
meaning into its amplitude or timing, ask:

1. **What is it referenced to?** A unipolar signal is measured against a distant electrode, so it
   includes far-field activity. For a bipolar signal, which electrode is distal? The sign depends on
   it (@eq-m03-bipolar).
2. **Which way was the wave going?** A bipole that lies across the wavefront records little,
   whatever the tissue (@eq-m03-bipolar-gradient). A second, crossing bipole or an omnipole (@eq-m03-omnipole) answers the question.
3. **What were the spacing, electrode size and height?** Together they set which spatial scales
   survive (cheat sheet, spatial filters).
4. **Is the signal local?** In this module's model, a close bipole peaks when the unipolar signal at
   its center falls fastest (Q6 above). Unipolar recordings taken at the same time are a useful
   check on bipolar ones [@stevenson2005].
5. **What filtering was applied?** High-pass filtering changes the shape of a unipolar signal
   [@stevenson2005]. Module m04 covers this.
6. **Do the model's assumptions hold here?** The markers derived in this module assume planar,
   uniform propagation. Near changes in activation sequence, curved fronts or non-uniform coupling
   they can mislead
   [@steinhaus1989; @riccio2021].

One sentence to keep: **a bipolar voltage is a property of the tissue, the catheter and the
wavefront together.**


## Cheat sheet

Everything here uses this module's model: a thin tissue sheet in an infinite homogeneous
conductor, a planar front with the arctangent profile, and point electrodes unless stated.
Throughout, $a = w + h$, and $s$ is the distance from the front to the electrode, positive before
the front arrives.

**Signals**

| Quantity | Result |
| ---------------- | ------------------------------------------------ |
| Unipolar potential (@eq-m03-volume-conductor) | $\phi = \frac{1}{4\pi\sigma} \iint \frac{i_m}{\lVert \mathbf r - \mathbf r' \rVert}\, dA'$ |
| Membrane current (@eq-m03-cable) | $i_m = \beta\, \partial^2 V_m / \partial x^2$ |
| Unipolar, planar front (@eq-m03-unipolar-closed) | $U(s) = A\, s/(s^2 + a^2)$. Peaks at $s = \pm a$, zero at $s = 0$, peak-to-peak $A/a$ |
| Unipolar timing (@eq-m03-unipolar-slope) | Peak to trough takes $2a/c$. Steepest slope $-cA/a^2$, at $s = 0$ |
| Activation marker (@eq-m03-intrinsic-deflection) | $t_{\text{act}} \approx \arg\max_t(-dU/dt)$. Exact only for ideal propagation |
| Bipolar (@eq-m03-bipolar) | $V_{\text{bip}} = \phi(\mathbf r_1) - \phi(\mathbf r_2)$, distal minus proximal |
| Close bipole, $d \ll a$ (@eq-m03-bipolar-gradient) | $V_{\text{bip}} \approx d\cos\theta\, \dfrac{dU}{ds} = -\dfrac{d \cos\theta}{c}\, \dfrac{dU}{dt}$ |
| Close-bipole amplitude | Peak-to-peak $\to \dfrac{9A}{8a^2}\, d\, \lvert\cos\theta\rvert$ |
| Clique field (@eq-m03-clique-field) | $\hat{\mathbf E} = -(D D^{\mathsf T})^{-1} D\, \mathbf b$. Needs three or more electrodes not in a line |
| Omnipole (@eq-m03-omnipole) | $v_\omega = -d\, \hat\omega \cdot \hat{\mathbf E}$ |
| Velocity from one clique (@eq-m03-clique-velocity) | $c \approx \mathrm{pp}(dU/dt) / \mathrm{pp}(\hat n \cdot \hat{\mathbf E})$ |

**Spatial filters** (spatial frequency $k$ in rad/mm)

| Element | Transfer function | Behavior |
| ----------- | ---------------- | ------------------ |
| Height $h$ | $e^{-\lvert k\rvert h}$ (@eq-m03-height-filter) | Low-pass |
| Disk electrode, radius $r_e$ | $2 J_1(k r_e)/(k r_e)$ (@eq-m03-disk-average) | Low-pass; first null at $k r_e \approx 3.83$ |
| Bipole, spacing $d$ | $2\lvert\sin(k d \cos\theta / 2)\rvert$ (@eq-m03-bipolar-transfer) | High-pass; peak at $k d\cos\theta = \pi$, nulls at multiples of $2\pi$ |
| Bipolar recording | Product of all three | Band-pass |

**Far field** from a source at distance $R \gg d$ (@eq-m03-farfield): for a monopole, the unipole
falls as $1/R$ and the bipole as $d/R^2$; for a dipole, as $1/R^2$ and $d/R^3$.

**What changes what** (close bipole, $d \ll a$)

| Change | Unipolar peak-to-peak | Unipolar steepest slope | Unipolar peak-to-trough time | Close-bipole peak-to-peak |
| ------------ | -------- | -------- | -------- | -------- |
| Double $a = w + h$ | Halves | Quarters | Doubles | Quarters |
| Double $c$ | Same | Doubles | Halves | Same |
| Double $d$ | Same | Same | Same | Doubles |
| Turn the bipole to angle $\theta$ | Same | Same | Same | Times $\lvert\cos\theta\rvert$ |

**Rules of thumb**

- A unipole sees near and far. A bipole sees near, along its own axis.
- In this model a small bipolar voltage can come from a weak source (small $A$), a large $w + h$,
  a short spacing, or a wave crossing the bipole near 90°. The voltage alone cannot tell these
  apart.
- Height and electrode size blur. Spacing decides which spatial scales a bipole keeps.
- An omnipole removes orientation dependence only while the clique is small next to $w + h$ and
  the wave is locally planar.
- Units: 1 m/s = 1 mm/ms, so a length in mm divided by a speed in m/s gives a time in ms.

## Interview questions

Try each question before you open its model answer. The answers use this module's model and
symbols. In a real interview, say which assumptions you are making.

### Fundamentals

**Q1. What does a unipolar electrogram measure, and why does a planar wavefront passing under the
electrode give a positive deflection followed by a negative one?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

It measures the potential at one electrode relative to a distant reference. By
@eq-m03-volume-conductor, that potential is a sum of membrane currents weighted by one over
distance. Ahead of the front, membrane current flows outward (a source); behind it, current flows
inward (a sink), and the two balance over the whole front. While the front approaches, the source
side is closer, so the potential is positive. When the front is directly under the electrode, the
two sides cancel and the potential crosses zero. After the front passes, the sink side is closer,
so the potential is negative. In closed form, $U(s) = A s/(s^2 + a^2)$: peaks at $s = \pm a$, zero
at $s = 0$ (@eq-m03-unipolar-closed).

</details>

**Q2. Why is the steepest negative slope of the unipolar signal used as the local activation time,
and when does that marker become unreliable?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

At a fixed electrode $dU/dt = -c\, dU/ds$ (@eq-m03-unipolar-slope). For the planar front $dU/ds$ is
largest at $s = 0$, so the steepest downstroke happens exactly when the front passes under the
electrode (@eq-m03-intrinsic-deflection). That holds for ideal, uniform propagation. Simulation
work found small errors under uniform conditions and larger ones near changes in activation
sequence, in short strands and with non-uniform coupling [@steinhaus1989]. Curved or colliding
fronts break the planar-wave assumption the derivation relies on.

</details>

**Q3. The electrode is lifted so that $w + h$ doubles. What happens to the unipolar amplitude, the
amplitude of a close bipole, and the signal duration? Which recording is more local, and why?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Unipolar peak-to-peak is $A/a$, so it halves. A close bipole's peak-to-peak is
$\frac{9A}{8a^2}\, d\, \lvert\cos\theta\rvert$, so it falls to a quarter. The unipolar peak-to-trough
time is $2a/c$, so it doubles: the signal gets smaller and broader. The bipole is more local:
its amplitude falls off faster with distance, so tissue close to the catheter dominates it. In
spatial-frequency terms, height multiplies the spectrum by $e^{-\lvert k\rvert h}$, and the bipole
mostly keeps the higher frequencies that this factor removes first (@eq-m03-height-filter).

</details>

**Q4. Describe a bipolar recording as a spatial filter. What sets its low and high edges, and
where are its nulls?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

A bipolar recording sees the tissue's current pattern through the product
$H_{\text{bip}} \cdot H_{\text{disk}} \cdot e^{-\lvert k\rvert h}$. The height factor and the disk
average $2J_1(kr_e)/(kr_e)$ are low-pass filters, so height and electrode size set the high edge:
fine detail is blurred, and the disk factor first reaches zero at $k r_e \approx 3.83$. The bipole
factor $2\lvert\sin(kd\cos\theta/2)\rvert$ is zero at $k = 0$, so spacing sets the low edge. It
peaks at $kd\cos\theta = \pi$ and has nulls wherever $kd\cos\theta$ is a multiple of $2\pi$ (@eq-m03-bipolar-transfer). Together they make a band-pass filter, and orientation enters through
$\cos\theta$.

</details>

### Derivation questions

**Q5. Show that a close bipole measures a directional derivative. How large is the error of that
approximation, and what does it predict about catheter orientation?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

For a planar wave the two electrodes sit at $s \pm \delta$, with $\delta = \tfrac{d}{2}\cos\theta$ (@eq-m03-bipolar-planar). A Taylor expansion gives
$U(s + \delta) - U(s - \delta) = 2\delta\, U'(s) + \tfrac{\delta^3}{3} U'''(s) + \dots$, so
$V_{\text{bip}} \approx d\cos\theta\, dU/ds = d\, \hat u \cdot \nabla\phi$ (@eq-m03-bipolar-gradient). The next term is smaller by a factor of order $\delta^2$, so the
relative error falls as $d^2$. The amplitude scales with $\lvert\cos\theta\rvert$: a bipole aligned
with the wave records the most, and one at 90° records nothing, because both electrodes activate
together. In animal recordings, voltage at the same site varied most where the wavefront was
perpendicular to one bipole and parallel to the other [@takigawa2018].

</details>

**Q6. Show that, in this model, a close bipolar electrogram is proportional to the time derivative
of the unipolar signal at its center. When does its largest value occur?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Combine $V_{\text{bip}} \approx d\cos\theta\, dU/ds$ (@eq-m03-bipolar-gradient) with
$dU/dt = -c\, dU/ds$ (@eq-m03-unipolar-slope):

$V_{\text{bip}}(t) \approx -\dfrac{d\cos\theta}{c}\, \dfrac{dU}{dt}$,

where $U$ is the unipolar signal at the bipole's center. The bipolar signal is largest in magnitude
when $-dU/dt$ is largest, which is when the front passes under the center of the bipole. So in the
ideal case, the bipolar peak and the unipolar steepest downstroke mark the same moment. The factor
$1/c$ cancels the factor $c$ in the slope, so the bipolar amplitude does not depend on conduction
velocity.

</details>

**Q7. Why do bipoles reject far-field activity better than unipoles? Derive the decay exponents,
and say why the rejection is never complete.**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

A distant source changes slowly across the catheter, so a bipole records about $d$ times the
gradient of its potential. A monopole's potential falls as $1/R$, so its gradient, and the bipole
signal, fall as $1/R^2$. A dipole's potential falls as $1/R^2$, so the bipole signal falls as
$1/R^3$ (@eq-m03-farfield). The bipole is always one power of $R$ better than the unipole. But the
gradient of a distant source is small, not zero, so far-field signals still appear in bipolar
recordings, and the local signal can lie under either electrode [@stevenson2005].

</details>

**Q8. How do you estimate the local electric field from a clique of electrodes, and what is the
smallest clique that works?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

If the potential is nearly linear across the clique, each bipole is a projection of the field:
$b_{ij} = \phi_j - \phi_i \approx -(\mathbf r_j - \mathbf r_i) \cdot \mathbf E$. Stacking the bipoles
gives $\mathbf b = -D^{\mathsf T}\mathbf E$, and least squares gives
$\hat{\mathbf E} = -(DD^{\mathsf T})^{-1} D\, \mathbf b$ [@riccio2021] (@eq-m03-clique-field). A
field in the plane has two unknowns, so the clique needs two independent bipole directions: at least
three electrodes that are not in a line. If the electrodes are collinear, $DD^{\mathsf T}$ has
rank 1, and only the field component along the line can be measured. A square clique gives six
bipoles for the same two unknowns, and least squares combines them.

</details>

**Q9. Derive the conduction velocity from a single clique, without measuring activation times.
Check the units.**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Along the propagation direction the field is $\hat n \cdot \mathbf E = -dU/ds$, and the unipolar
slope is $dU/dt = -c\, dU/ds$ (@eq-m03-unipolar-slope). Dividing one by the other cancels $dU/ds$,
so $c \approx \mathrm{pp}(dU/dt)/\mathrm{pp}(\hat n \cdot \hat{\mathbf E})$ (@eq-m03-clique-velocity) [@riccio2021; @deno2017]. Units: (mV/ms) divided by (mV/mm) is mm/ms,
which equals m/s. The estimate assumes a plane wave across the clique and that the unipolar signal
is recorded at the clique. Module m25 returns to conduction velocity.

</details>

### Design and troubleshooting

**Q10. At one site, the bipolar amplitude halves after the catheter is rotated, and nothing else
changes. Give a model explanation, and say how you would tell an orientation effect from a real
change in the tissue.**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

For a close bipole the amplitude scales with $\lvert\cos\theta\rvert$ (@eq-m03-bipolar-gradient).
If the bipole was aligned with the wave before, halving means $\lvert\cos\theta\rvert$ went from 1 to
0.5, which is a rotation of 60° relative to the propagation direction. To separate orientation
from tissue: look at the unipolar amplitude, which a point electrode records independently of
catheter orientation; compare several bipole directions at the same site; or use an omnipolar
estimate, which, within its assumptions, reads the field along the propagation direction whatever
the catheter's orientation (@eq-m03-omnipole).

</details>

**Q11. For a fixed local wavefront and a fixed distant source, how does bipole spacing change the
share of far-field signal in a bipolar recording?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

While $d \ll a$, both the local and the far-field bipolar signals are about $d$ times a gradient,
so their ratio barely depends on $d$. Once $d$ is comparable to $a = w + h$, the local signal stops
growing: the bipole spans the whole front, and for very wide spacing it records two separate
unipolar deflections, with peak-to-peak tending to $A/a$. The far-field term keeps growing with $d$
as long as $d \ll R$. So wider spacing raises the far-field share. In this model, with a monopole at
$R = 200a$ on the bipole axis, the share stays within 1% of the short-bipole value up to
$d = 0.2a$. It is about 1.2 times that value at $d = a$, and about 1.9 times at $d = 2a$.

</details>

**Q12. Why is an omnipolar amplitude independent of catheter orientation, and which assumptions
break that?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

The clique estimates the field vector $\hat{\mathbf E}$, whichever bipoles the catheter happens to
offer. Reading it along the propagation direction gives the signal of a bipole aligned with the
wave, whatever the catheter's orientation (@eq-m03-omnipole). That relies on a locally planar wave
and a potential that is linear across the clique. Both fail as the spacing grows relative to
$w + h$. In this model, without time alignment, the spread of omnipolar amplitude across wave
directions grows from under 1% at $d/a = 0.2$ to about 32% at $d/a = 1.6$ for a square clique.
Published work traces the same bias to bipoles in a clique activating at slightly different times,
and aligning them first reduces it [@riccio2021]. Curved or colliding fronts make the field trace a
true loop, and then no single direction describes propagation.

</details>

**Q13. In this model, does slower conduction lower unipolar or bipolar voltage? What does it
change?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Not on its own. With $w$, $h$ and the source strength fixed, the signal is $U(x_e - ct)$, so $c$
only rescales the time axis. Unipolar peak-to-peak stays $A/a$, and close-bipole peak-to-peak stays
$\frac{9A}{8a^2}\, d\, \lvert\cos\theta\rvert$. What changes is timing: the unipolar peak-to-trough
time $2a/c$ grows, and the steepest slope $cA/a^2$ falls, as $c$ falls. In this model, a voltage
change has to come from $A$, $w$, $h$, $d$ or $\theta$. The model treats those as independent of
$c$. Whether they stay fixed when conduction slows in real tissue depends on why it slows; module
m09 covers propagation.

</details>

## Code lab

The lab rebuilds this module's results in code, so you can see where each one comes from and
break it on purpose. It runs in about a minute.

| Part | What you do | Data |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | Compute a unipolar electrogram by summing the volume-conductor integral, check it against @eq-m03-unipolar-closed, and find the activation marker | synthetic |
| B | Rotate a bipole and measure when the $\lvert\cos\theta\rvert$ rule holds | synthetic |
| C | Treat height and the bipole as spatial filters with FFTs (@eq-m03-height-filter, @eq-m03-bipolar-transfer) | synthetic |
| D | Estimate the field from a clique, build an omnipole, and get conduction velocity from one clique (@eq-m03-clique-velocity) | synthetic |
| E | Look at real bipolar recordings from a decapolar catheter and estimate delays between neighboring bipoles | PhysioNet |

- **Python notebook:**
  [labs/python/m03_lab.ipynb]({{< var repo.url >}}/blob/main/labs/python/m03_lab.ipynb).
  Run it from the course repository after `pip install -r requirements.txt`, or
  [open it in Google Colab]({{< var repo.colab >}}/blob/main/labs/python/m03_lab.ipynb).
- **GNU Octave or MATLAB:**
  [labs/octave/m03_lab.m]({{< var repo.url >}}/blob/main/labs/octave/m03_lab.m)
  covers parts A–D with the same checks. It needs no toolboxes.
- **Data for part E:** one record (about 1 MB) of the Intracardiac Atrial Fibrillation Database
  [@iafdb; @goldberger2000], downloaded from PhysioNet and checked against PhysioNet's published
  SHA-256 checksums. License: Open Data Commons Attribution v1.0. Without internet access, part E
  is skipped.

Each part ends with **checks**: lines that pass with the code as given. If you change something
and a check fails, that is information, not an error to hide.

## Self-check

Short checks you can do in your head. Open each answer after you have tried it.

**S1. A planar front moves at 1.0 m/s past an electrode with $w + h$ = 1.3 mm (the module's
defaults). How long after the positive peak of the unipolar electrogram does its negative trough
come?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

$2a/c$ = 2 × 1.3 mm ÷ 1.0 mm/ms = 2.6 ms (1 m/s = 1 mm/ms). See the cheat sheet, unipolar timing.

</details>

**S2. A close bipole aligned with the wave is turned by 60°. What fraction of its amplitude is
left? What about at 90°?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

$\lvert\cos 60°\rvert$ = 0.5, so half. At 90° both electrodes activate together, and in this model
the bipole records nothing (@eq-m03-bipolar-gradient).

</details>

**S3. A 2-mm bipole lies along the propagation direction. Which spatial wavelength does it cancel
completely, and which does it pass best?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

$\lvert H_{\text{bip}}\rvert = 2\lvert\sin(kd/2)\rvert$ is zero when $kd = 2\pi$, which is a
wavelength $\lambda = 2\pi/k$ equal to the spacing: 2 mm (and 1 mm, 0.67 mm, ...). It is largest
when $kd = \pi$, at $\lambda = 2d$ = 4 mm (@eq-m03-bipolar-transfer).

</details>

**S4. A distant point source moves twice as far away. By what factor do its unipolar and bipolar
signals fall?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

The unipolar signal falls as $1/R$, so by 2. The bipolar signal falls as $1/R^2$, so by 4 (@eq-m03-farfield).

</details>

**S5. A disk electrode has radius 0.5 mm (demo m03-d3's default). At what spatial wavelength does
its averaging first cancel a pattern completely?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

The disk factor $2J_1(kr_e)/(kr_e)$ first reaches zero at $kr_e \approx 3.83$, so
$k \approx 7.66$ rad/mm, and $\lambda = 2\pi/k \approx 0.82$ mm (@eq-m03-disk-average).

</details>

**S6. Which of these does the single-clique estimate of conduction velocity *not* need?**
(a) the unipolar slope $dU/dt$; (b) the field along the propagation direction; (c) local
activation times; (d) a wave that is planar across the clique.

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

(c). The estimate is the ratio $\mathrm{pp}(dU/dt)/\mathrm{pp}(\hat n \cdot \hat{\mathbf E})$, which
needs no activation times, but it does assume a planar wave across the clique (@eq-m03-clique-velocity).

</details>

**S7. True or false: in this model, halving the conduction velocity halves the bipolar voltage.**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

False. With $w$, $h$ and the source fixed, $c$ only stretches time: the voltage stays the same,
the signal lasts twice as long, and slopes halve (interview Q13).

</details>


## Literature figures

These figures are worth looking at alongside this module. We link to them instead of copying
them: some licenses do not allow reuse here, and others we could not confirm. Each entry says what
to look for and where this module explains it.

- **Electric-field loops with and without time alignment.** Riccio and colleagues, Figure 5
  [@riccio2021; [free full text](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8446360/)]. It shows
  bipolar electrograms and field loops for square and triangular cliques, with and without time
  alignment of the bipoles, for plane and curved wavefronts at three catheter orientations.
  Compare plane with curved fronts, and aligned with unaligned bipoles. In this module a plane wave
  traces a line along the propagation direction (@eq-m03-omnipole), and spacing that is large next
  to $w + h$ distorts it (demo m03-d5).
- **Bipolar voltage maps in two orientations.** Magtibay and colleagues, Figure 2
  [@magtibay2017; [free full text](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5586472/)]. Bipolar
  electrograms and voltage maps from a rabbit, a pig and a human heart, along two perpendicular
  electrode orientations, with maps built from the larger bipole. Compare the two orientations
  for the same **pacing** site (the place the heart was stimulated from). This module's explanation is the $\lvert\cos\theta\rvert$ rule
  (@eq-m03-bipolar-gradient, demo m03-d2, interview Q10).
- **Thresholds and lesions.** Magtibay and colleagues, Figure 8 [@magtibay2017]. Omnipolar voltage
  maps with a threshold set from ablation lesions in pig hearts, compared with maps using the
  traditional bipolar dense-scar cut-off of 0.5 mV. It goes with the clinical correlate above.
- **The upstroke behind the front model.** Loose and colleagues, Figure 3 [@loose2014;
  [free full text, CC BY 3.0](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3940943/)]. Original
  action-potential recordings from human right atrial tissue, one preparation per patient group.
  Look at how brief the upstroke is next to the rest of the action potential. @eq-m03-front keeps
  only the upstroke, compressed into a front of width $w$; the m03-d1 assumptions derive $w$ from
  this study's amplitude.


## Further reading

- **Theory.** @plonsey2007: a textbook on bioelectricity, including the volume-conductor theory
  behind @eq-m03-volume-conductor.
- **Recording practice.** @stevenson2005: a short review of unipolar and bipolar recording,
  filtering and sampling in the electrophysiology lab. @debakker2019: a review of electrogram
  recording and analysis techniques for choosing ablation target sites.
- **Omnipolar signals.** @deno2017: the engineering paper that introduced omnipolar signals from
  electric-field loops and tested them in a saline tank. @masse2016: omnipolar conduction velocity
  checked against optical and electrical mapping in several models. @riccio2021: a simulation study
  of omnipolar strategies with square and triangular cliques, time alignment and noise.
  @magtibay2019: a review of what omnipolar electrograms add to mapping.
- **Voltage.** @anter2016: an editorial on what bipolar voltage amplitude means.
